abstract: Asthma is a heterogeneous airway disease in which chronic inflammation, epithelial barrier injury, immune-cell imbalance and airway remodeling interact to shape variable clinical phenotypes. N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic mRNA, has emerged as a dynamic epitranscriptomic layer that regulates RNA splicing, export, stability, translation and decay. Recent profiling studies and mechanistic experiments indicate that m6A patterns and m6A regulators are altered in lung tissue, airway epithelial cells, airway smooth muscle cells and immune cells in asthma. These changes influence type 2 inflammation, the balance between T helper 1 (Th1) and T helper 2 (Th2) cells, the balance between T helper 17 (Th17) and regulatory T (Treg) cells, macrophage polarization, epithelial ferroptosis, ciliary function, mitochondrial stress, pollutant responses and structural remodeling. This Review synthesizes current evidence linking m6A writers, erasers and readers to asthma pathobiology, highlights context-dependent and sometimes opposing functions of key regulators such as METTL3, FTO and ALKBH5, and discusses how m6A signatures may inform biomarker discovery and therapeutic development. We also outline major translational barriers, including cell-type specificity, target validation, assay standardization and safety of pharmacologic m6A modulation.

Type="plain-language-summary" Language="eng"><AbstractText>Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways become inflamed and narrow, making it harder to breathe. It is influenced by airway cells, immune cells and factors in the environment. This review focuses on m6A, a small chemical tag added to RNA, which helps cells use genetic information. Changes in m6A may affect how airway and immune cells behave and may contribute to persistent inflammation, airway damage and changes in lung structure. In the future, this knowledge may help distinguish different types of asthma and guide the development of new tests and treatments. However, more research in people with asthma is needed before these findings can be used in routine care.</AbstractText></OtherAbstract><KeywordList Owner="NOTNLM"><Keyword MajorTopicYN="N">Asthma</Keyword><Keyword MajorTopicYN="N">RNA methylation</Keyword><Keyword MajorTopicYN="N">epitranscriptome</Keyword><Keyword MajorTopicYN="N">immunoregulation</Keyword><Keyword MajorTopicYN="N">m6A modification</Keyword></KeywordList><CoiStatement>The authors have no relevant affiliations or financial involvement with any organization or entity with a financial interest in or financial conflict with the subject matter or materials discussed in the manuscript.
